methodological_rigor.justification: The study leverages a large (n=139,120) general-population Dutch cohort (Lifelines) linked to the Netherlands Cancer Registry with ICD-10-verified outcomes, evaluating three traditional criteria (NLST, NELSON, USPSTF-2021) and five externally published risk models (LLPv2, PLCOm2012, Hoggart, Bach, Shanghai-LCM). Calibration (E/O ratios) and discrimination (AUC) are both reported. Limitations include self-reported smoking, 42% linkage coverage (explicit selection-bias risk), rescaling of the Bach 10-year model to 5 years, and threshold harmonization for some models based on LLPv2-matched eligibility rather than pre-specified thresholds. Statistical approach is appropriate (Chi-square, AUC, E/O ratios, assumed trial-derived mortality reductions) though no confidence intervals are given for AUCs and no bootstrapped comparisons between models.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is an individual prospective cohort study used for external validation of prognostic/screening models, mapping to Oxford LoE 2b. Clinical relevance is direct: findings demonstrate that 57.8-81.6% of lung cancers within 5 years in a Western European general population occur in individuals ineligible under current criteria, providing actionable evidence for refining screening policy (age thresholds, time-since-quitting). The work also provides the first external validation of the Shanghai-LCM model in a European cohort.

reporting_quality.justification: As an external validation of prediction models, TRIPOD applies. The paper clearly reports participant flow, predictors, thresholds, calibration, discrimination, and sensitivity/specificity for each model, and acknowledges limitations (overestimation, linkage incompleteness, self-report). Formal TRIPOD checklist adherence is not explicitly declared. Data availability is limited: Lifelines and NCR data require governed access, individual-level data cannot be shared, and analysis scripts are not clearly deposited.

novelty_literature.justification: Prior work has compared PLCOm2012 and LLPv2 in UK and other European cohorts (refs 7, 18, 20) and has highlighted ineligible-cancer populations (refs 21-23). The novel contributions are the broad comparison of five risk models plus three criteria in a large unselected Dutch general population, and the first external validation of Shanghai-LCM in a European population. These are meaningful incremental advances but do not constitute a paradigm shift.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well organized with clear sections, accessible tables, and appropriate use of supplementary materials. Sentences are generally precise, abbreviations are defined, and the discussion carefully contextualizes findings against prior cohorts. Minor issues include slightly repetitive framing of the 'ineligible cases' message and occasional awkward phrasing ('Patents' section heading appears to be mislabeled, likely 'Patient involvement').

key_strengths: Very large (n=139,120) general-population cohort linked to a high-quality national cancer registry
Comprehensive head-to-head comparison of three criteria and five risk models including the first European validation of Shanghai-LCM
Policy-relevant finding that 57.8-81.6% of 5-year lung cancers occur in individuals ineligible under current criteria
Calibration and discrimination metrics both reported, with explicit characterization of ineligible-case populations
key_concerns: Only 42% linkage between Lifelines and NCR raises selection bias concerns
Bach model rescaled from 10-year to 5-year horizon; threshold harmonization relies on LLPv2 eligibility matching
Self-reported smoking data and no confidence intervals on AUCs or formal model comparisons
TRIPOD checklist adherence not explicitly declared
No data/code availability plan beyond referencing restricted cohort access
chief_reviewer.rationale: Solid, policy-relevant external validation of multiple lung cancer screening models in a large general-population European cohort; methodological gaps are minor and the clinical message is clearly supported, fitting a tier-2 oncology or thoracic specialty journal.
